turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning. It's the ankles, yes?

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, both of them. Three weeks they've been up, I'd say, and I was telling Linda, she lives in, she's my carer, it's not like the hip, that was only the left one, this is the pair, and by the evening they're like puddings, I can't get the brown shoes near me.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Two weeks, doctor, not three. I noticed the Monday before last, her slippers were tight.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Two or three weeks, then. Are you breathless?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): On the stairs I am. I get halfway and I have to hang on the rail. Sat down I'm fine, I watched a whole gardening programme and never puffed once.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Breathless lying flat at night?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Linda makes tea about nine, we have the plain digestives, not the chocolate, and I doze in the chair by the window, the stair carpet's loose on the third step you see.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): In bed. Breathless, yes or no?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): No. The bed's alright. Two pillows, same as always.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes. Not really. More a niggle if I've done the stairs, I wouldn't call it pain, not like my sister, she had the spray and all that.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Cough?

[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough now. I did have one on the ramipril, but the hospital doctor stopped that. I can't remember the dose, it was a pinkish thing, capsule or tablet, I wouldn't like to say.
[SEG0014] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Ramipril was stopped in March by the cardiologist, because of the cough. She hasn't had it since.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Who sorts the tablets?
[SEG0016] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I do. I live in. I fill the box every Sunday.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): What's she taking?

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): The little white one in the morning, and another little white one for the blood pressure, and the water tablet for the swelling, forty milligrams every morning, I never miss it. The ramipril's gone, as I said, and my neighbour, not your patient, her box is the size of a biscuit tin, honestly.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Carer, the proper list.

[SEG0020] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The little white one is bisoprolol, two and a half milligrams, once each morning. She's counting it twice. There isn't a second little white tablet. Amlodipine is the blood pressure one, five milligrams, once a day, and it's a bit bigger.
[SEG0021] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I have never put two bisoprolol in. Just the one.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the water tablet?
[SEG0023] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Furosemide. The tablets at home are twenty milligrams, and she gets one in the morning. Not forty.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): The doctor before told me forty. There's an old packet in the drawer under the tea towels, I'm sure it says forty on it. I've said forty for years.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the dose isn't agreed. Does she take it every day?
[SEG0026] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Most days. If she's going to the hairdresser she sometimes won't have it. I can't promise it's every day.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): I do take it. Only if we're out I skip it, because the toilets in town are shut, and I don't want to be stuck. Not often. Thursdays, mostly.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No, none. I had penicillin as a girl and not so much as a rash, so no allergies at all.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ankles worse by the end of the day?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, both, right up to the shins by teatime. They're nearly down in the morning. Feet on the pouffe helps a bit, that was Linda.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any weight gain?

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): My daughter in Bristol is forever saying have more soup, she rings on a Sunday, she's not the carer, Linda isn't family, and leek and potato is my favourite, with a bit of bread.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure is 152 over 88. Pulse 64.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): There's pitting oedema in both legs, up to the mid-shin. Chest is clear, no crackles.

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): So is it the heart? I've had the heart failure for years, and the blood pressure too. They said the heart was tired when I had the left hip replaced, twenty fourteen, at the infirmary.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. Known heart failure, and high blood pressure. I'd say the fluid is building up again. Working impression only.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm changing the water tablet. Furosemide forty milligrams, one each morning, new prescription. Stop the twenty milligram ones.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Right, so the twenties are finished.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. I want a kidney function blood test this week, with the dose change.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Will that be at this surgery? The parking was dreadful last time, Linda went round three times, and I'd the winter coat on, much too hot in that waiting room.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, here. Legs up when you sit. Don't add salt. If you're gasping, or the swelling shoots up, ring us the same day.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll see you in two weeks. Bring the boxes.
[SEG0044] person_3 (CAREGIVER): We'll bring the boxes.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, yes. And I'll have a go at taking the tablet on Thursdays too, if the toilets allow.

clinical_actions.description: Prescribe furosemide 40 mg once each morning and stop the 20 mg tablets
Kidney function blood test this week at this surgery
Elevate the legs when sitting and avoid added salt
Ring the same day if gasping or the swelling increases rapidly
Follow-up consultation
Bring the medication boxes to the next visit

clinical_uncertainties.description: The patient said the ankle swelling had lasted three weeks and the carer said two weeks, and the doctor left it as two or three weeks.
The patient says the water tablet is 40 mg and the carer says the tablets at home are 20 mg furosemide, one in the morning and not 40 mg, so the current dose is not agreed.

The carer says the water tablet is sometimes missed, including hairdresser days, and cannot promise it is every day, and the patient says she skips it when out, mostly on Thursdays, so daily adherence is uncertain.
